description.narrative:
The reason of this booking is that the operational costs of the implementing partner under A-06724-04 project was not budgeted for, simultaneously it was not conceivable for Oxfam to ask the donor to amend the approved budget hence there was a need to use this project and allocate the operational cost using the appeal fund linked to this project OXF3208.01. Below is the project summary of A-06724 Food insecurity is expected to worsen in 2021 across Somalia – particularly in our target regions of Sool, Sanaag, Bari and Nugal - driven by below-average rainfall and a worsening desert locust infestation. According to the post-Deyr seasonal food security and nutrition assessment by FSNAU-FEWS Net (Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit – Famine Early Warning Systems Network), up to 2.7 million people across Somalia are expected to face food consumption gaps or depletion of livelihood assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes through mid-2021 in the absence of humanitarian assistance.This constitutes a stark increase compared to the findings from last year’s Ppost-Deyyr assessment: the number of people predicted to be in IPC Phase 3 or worse has doubled over the course of only one year – from 1.3 in 2020 to 2.7 million in 2021. Approximately 1.6 million people face phase (3) “Crisis” or worse outcomes in the presence of planned and likely humanitarian assistance during the January-March 2021 period. An additional 2.9 million people are expected to be under food stress, bringing the total number of people facing acute food insecurity to 5.6million.
The price of water in the local market has more than doubled in between October2020 and March 2021. According to Oxfam’s own market assessment in Eastern Somaliland (Sool and Sanaag), one barrel of water is currently being sold at an average of 4.5 USD per barrel, with some villages reporting over 7 USD per barrel. This is forcing the most vulnerable households to travel long distances to fetch water and/or opt for poor water quality andrisk their lives. The most affected communities include IDPs and low-income host communities.
Women and girls are at high risk of harassment, rape and attacks by wild animals as they travel far in search of water for their families, as also highlightedby Oxfam Somalia’s most recent gender analyses conducted in late 2020 in Somaliland andPuntland. Sexual violence and other forms of gender-basedviolence are widespread and remained under reported; victims/survivors become subject to stigmatization andsecondary victimization. GBV and VAW (Violence against Women) increased after coronavirus as a result of economic stress. Women’s responsibilitiesathousehold level became more demanding. There is a heavy dependence on the men of the family for the protectionof the women and girls.
Furthermore, Somalia is being affected badly by the third wave of COVID-19. An average of 16-19% of people testedarecurrently positive. As of 19 March 2021, over 9,600 cases with 392 fatalities have been reportedby the SomaliaMinistry of Health and WHO. Given the low capacity of testing and stigmatization in Somalia, it is suspected that thecaseload might be much higher than the reported numbers.
Somalia has the fourth largest population of internally displaced peopleinthe world, driven by protracted and cyclical conflict and insecurity, and drought and floods. Many IDPs and urban poor live in congested conditions with inadequate access to basic services and public health. Rapid urbanization has seen some IDPs move from rural areas to cities in search of shelter, protection and humanitarian assistance, with cities struggling to cope with the needs of both urban poor and internally displaced populations whose squalid, congested living conditions heighten COVID-19 risks.Forced eviction ofIDPs from homes or land which they occupy against their will and without legal protection is both a cause and multiplierof displacement. Droughts, locust and the socioeconomic and health impacts of COVID-19 are expected to remain until 2022-2023, further weakening the coping capacity of communities unless the underlying causes of these vulnerabilities are addressed. Thisprojectis aimed to tackle the triple crises and contribute to saving lives and restoring livelihoods via integrated WASH-,EFSVL- and protection programming

participating-org.narrative: It is a Somali women non-governmental humanitarian organization at a national level founded in 1992 at Mogadishu - the capital city, by a group of Somali women intellectuals from cross-section of the community. The Save Somali Women and Children (SSWC) contributeto the creation of a safe and sustainable situation by supporting women to overcome marginalization, violence and poverty in their communities. It operates as a non-profit making organization that has the right to network with a variety of organizations that share similar values and vision. In Somalia women face a range of complex challenges that require multiple solutions. We work in the belief that women through their own efforts and in collaboration with local, national and international allies are central to transforming their own lives and the lives of their communities and population of which they are part. SSWC is women-led and women-centered organization (so its programs reflect the needs of those served) that have well functioning management, finance and programmatic structures and systems.
